$comment: Single source of truth for canonical user attributes and provider claim mappings. Used by the Go IdP, the TypeScript wallet and the auth SDK. Attribute keys follow OIDC Standard Claims (RFC 7519 §5.1). 'verifiable' = can reach 'provider' assurance (an OIDC claim like email_verified); 'identityVerifiable' = the identity-verifier enclave (passport/ID + biometric) can evidence this attribute, either because the key IS the government-backed one or because it has one (see $assuranceComment). 'multiValued' = the wallet may hold more than one value (e.g. several emails); on import a differing value is added alongside rather than treated as a conflict. Assurance levels: none < provider < gov (see kyc-enclave-design.md §3).
$assuranceComment: ASSURANCE IS A PROPERTY OF THE KEY. A first name the holder typed and a first name read off their passport are two DIFFERENT attributes at two prices and two trust levels, so they get two keys: 'given_name' is the self-asserted (or social-IdP-sourced) one and 'given_name_id' is the government-ID-backed one, each with its own marketplace row. The '_id' suffix is the whole convention — it exists only where a self-asserted twin exists to be told apart from, which is why the document-only fields (document_number, sex, issuing_state, doc_expiry, ...) keep bare names. 'assurance' states the key's own level in the registry's vocabulary ('self_asserted' / 'gov_verified'); when absent it is 'gov_verified' for an identity-scope key and 'self_asserted' otherwise, but every identity-scope key spells it out so a future gov attribute outside that scope cannot arrive silently under-assured. 'govKey' points from a self-asserted key to its government-backed twin, and is what makes adding a pair cheap: name the twin, add the '_id' row, done. 'birthdate' and 'nationality' predate the convention and were minted government-backed; they are now dual like the rest, so the bare key is the self-asserted reading and 'birthdate_id' / 'nationality_id' carry the government-backed one. That split is a BREAKING change for anything that named the bare key expecting a passport value, which is why it ships with the migrations that rewrite a registered client's required_attributes (auth idp store, management-service 077). 'supersededBy' is the schema's answer to a key that is genuinely retired rather than paired; no key carries it today, and a pair is almost always the better answer. NEVER delete or rename a key that has shipped: a relying party's registration, a stored share link and a signed voucher all name it verbatim. 'requestOnly' keeps a key out of every scope-derived set: the relying party must name it, in its required_attributes whitelist (within the scope that would have carried it) or in the per-request 'attributes' parameter. It is the fail-closed half of the model and it is set on every '_id' key, so a client that asks for 'identity' and nothing else never acquires a billable disclosure it did not name. Pricing a key therefore MEANS making it request-only, in the same change: doc_expiry, place_of_birth and personal_number rode the identity scope for free until migration 076 priced them, and leaving them there would have charged every identity request for three disclosures nobody asked for. 'certifiedField' is the identity-verifier field prove_field opens for the key, when it differs from the key ('given_name_id' opens the passport's 'given_name' commitment; the storage spelling would be rejected as uncertified). 'disclosure' is 'token' (the default for a gov key: a short-lived enclave-signed SD-JWT VC produced by commit-and-prove) or 'raw' for a gov-SOURCED value the enclave will not re-certify as a disclosure, where the wallet relays its stored copy so a relying party gets provenance but no fresh signature; a 'raw' key is therefore never billable. No key is 'raw' today: the DG2 portrait was, until identity-verifier v0.6.3 committed to it under its own salt and made 'picture_id' provable. 'derived' marks a key with no stored value at all: the enclave computes it from the identity receipt at disclosure time (document_valid, age_band), so its absence from the profile is not a missing attribute and the wallet must never prompt for it. age_over_18/21 are deliberately NOT derived — the wallet does store the boolean it computed at import, and consent screens show it.
$marketplaceComment: 'marketplace' is present on exactly those attributes the attribute marketplace can issue as a paid disclosure, and exists so that no component reconstructs the namespaced key by hand. 'key' is the '<namespace>:<name>' form the IdP requests, the voucher names and a billing grant must match verbatim: a reservation resolves attributes by namespace and refuses a bare name, so the two spellings are not interchangeable. It is NOT 'privasys:' + the canonical key: the registry names the field the ENCLAVE meters, which for an '_id' key is its 'certifiedField' — 'given_name_id' is sold as 'privasys:given_name' because that is the string /prove/field puts on the meter. 'billable' says a disclosure carries a charge at all; the PRICE is deliberately absent. The registry (management-service migrations 055/056, table 'attributes') stays authoritative for price, status and for third-party namespaces, which this file cannot know about — read the live catalogue when the price or the full provider list matters. Absence of the block means the attribute is never billed, and that is the fail-closed rule: an attribute with no registry row must never be namespaced for billing, because a reservation naming an unknown key fails the whole authorization. Adding a block is therefore the SECOND of two steps: migration 076 seeded doc_expiry, place_of_birth, personal_number and picture_id, which identity-verifier v0.6.3 had already made certifiable, and only then did they gain one here.
